item.title: Trump's Smart Iran Exit
item.description: Jon Alterman argues in the Times of India that Trump was right to end the Iran war, not because the U.S. won, but because the conflict exposed the limits of military power, reshaped U.S.-Israel ties, and showed the value of diplomacy and partners like India.

item.title: Venezuela Suffered Its Worst Earthquake in Decades: What Comes Next?
item.description: Two powerful earthquakes, measuring 7.2 and 7.5 on the Richter scale, recently struck along the coast of Venezuela. The international response will be a major test of U.S. leadership and Washington's new relationship with Caracas.

item.title: Lebanon in the Shadow of the U.S.-Iran MOU: Risks and Opportunities
item.description: The diplomacy underway to end the U.S.-Israel-Iran war could deepen Lebanon's strategic setbacks—or it could provide a historic opportunity to advance key Lebanese interests and contribute to a more stable regional order.

item.title: Preventing Iran’s Military Reconstitution
item.description: Iran’s ability to reconstitute its military depends on its ability to import key materials and equipment. With the UAE’s role as Iran’s central reexport hub up in the air, policymakers have a narrow window to identify and disrupt new procurement routes as they take shape.

item.title: After Maduro: Human Trafficking and the Vulnerability of Venezuelan Migrants in Colombia
item.description: The fragile security situations in both Colombia and Venezuela create conditions that allow criminal and non-state armed groups to expand trafficking in persons.

item.title: Entity List Additions Cool to Their Slowest Pace Since 2008
item.description: Thelack of additions to the Entity Listsince October 2025 marks a sharp break from years of U.S. geoeconomic strategy. Due to the continually shifting nature of procurement networks,a list that stops expanding tracks fewer relevant actors, eroding its value as a control.

item.title: The Heat Tax: India, South Asia, and the New Economics of Heat Readiness
item.description: Extreme heat is no longer a seasonal hardship in South Asia; it's a structural economic constraint. India lost 247 billion potential labor hours to heat in 2024. The question is whether governments and investors will fund prevention before the losses become unavoidable.

item.title: Don’t Let the USMCA Drift Away
item.description: On July 1, North America’s trade pact comes up for review. The real risk isn’t collapse, but rather the slow, expensive erosion already underway.

item.title: South Korea’s Market Boom—and the Bubble Beneath It
item.description: The South Korean stock market is the world’s best-performing in the first six months of 2026, doubling in value mainly on investors’ perceptions of two companies. But South Korean investors are also at great risk because the euphoric sentiment driving the rally will end someday. This could shock the broader economy, create political fallout, and damage Koreans’ confidence in stock investing.

item.description: CSIS Americas Program Senior Associate Evan Ellis unpacks the governance crisis in Bolivia and its implications for President Rodrigo Paz, regional democratic stability, and the U.S. “Shield of the Americas” alliance.

item.title: Fortress North America: Mexico’s Role in Securing the Region’s Economic Future
item.description: The 2026 USMCA review is the first test of whether the United States, Mexico, and Canada can turn economic security into a regional framework. Mexico is the hinge, as the top U.S. trading partner, but is also importing from China at a 14-to-1 ratio.

item.title: Russian Blood and Treasure: The Ballooning Costs of Putin’s War
item.description: Russia has suffered approximately 1.4 million casualties and 450,000 fatalities in Ukraine for only marginal territorial gains, according to new CSIS data. In addition, Ukraine has conducted deep strikes into Russian territory, including with AI-enabled drones.
